title: Ezekiel 18:1–20
context: The LORD rejects a proverb used in Israel: the fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge. He declares that all souls belong to him and that the soul who sins will die. Through a sequence of cases (a righteous man, his violent son, and that son’s righteous son) he shows that each person stands before him according to his own ways. Jeremiah 31:29-30 cites the same proverb. Deuteronomy 24:16 and the warnings of Exodus 20:5 and Deuteronomy 5:9 are often read alongside the chapter, and each can be heard in its own setting. Both traditions affirm personal accountability here, and neither treats the chapter as denying the solidarity of humanity in sin (compare Romans 5:12).

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me again, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word came to me again, saying, Arminian readers note that the LORD addresses the prophet with a new message, this time answering a saying circulating among the people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the chapter begins, like many in Ezekiel, with the word coming to the prophet. What follows is a sustained argument rather than a vision or sign-act.

verses.text: “What do you mean, that you use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge’?
verses.arminianNotes: What do you mean, that you use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, Arminian readers see the LORD rejecting a fatalistic excuse that blamed the previous generation; each generation is accountable and, by grace, free to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the proverb rejected as an evasion of responsibility, without denying humanity’s solidarity in sin (compare Romans 5:12). Both read it with Jeremiah 31:29-30, which cites the same proverb.

verses.text: “As I live,” says the Lord GOD, “you shall not use this proverb any more in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: you shall not use this proverb any more in Israel. Arminian readers see the LORD’s oath putting an end to the proverb, so that no one may hide behind the sins of others or treat judgment as inherited fate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD swears by his own life, the strongest assurance in Scripture. The proverb will not survive because the LORD has spoken against it under oath.

verses.text: Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul who sins, he shall die.
verses.arminianNotes: Behold, all souls are mine; Arminian readers see each person related directly to God, father and son alike, so that each answers for his own life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the LORD’s ownership of every soul and the principle that the one who sins will die for it. Both traditions affirm this as shared ground about personal accountability.

verses.text: “But if a man is just, and does that which is lawful and right,
verses.arminianNotes: But if a man is just, and does that which is lawful and right, Arminian readers see the first case: a man whose life shows covenant faithfulness in concrete actions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that just here describes covenant loyalty expressed in conduct, not sinless perfection. The list that follows gives examples of what such a life looks like.

verses.text: and has not eaten on the mountains, hasn’t lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, hasn’t defiled his neighbor’s wife, hasn’t come near a woman in her impurity,
verses.arminianNotes: hasn’t lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, Arminian readers see faithfulness in worship and in personal purity, refusing idols and honoring his neighbor’s marriage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that eating on the mountains is commonly read as sharing in meals at idolatrous shrines. The verse joins worship and sexual ethics as parts of the same faithfulness.

verses.text: and has not wronged any, but has restored to the debtor his pledge, has taken nothing by robbery, has given his bread to the hungry, and has covered the naked with a garment;
verses.arminianNotes: and has not wronged any, Arminian readers see justice toward the poor: returning the debtor’s pledge, refraining from robbery, feeding the hungry, and clothing the naked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the law’s concern for the vulnerable runs through the list. True righteousness is shown not only in avoiding wrong but in active mercy.

verses.text: he who hasn’t lent to them with interest, hasn’t taken any increase from them, who has withdrawn his hand from iniquity, has executed true justice between man and man,
verses.arminianNotes: he who hasn’t lent to them with interest, Arminian readers see economic justice as part of faithfulness, refusing to profit from the need of a neighbor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the man has executed true justice between man and man. The law of Moses forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19), and Ezekiel applies it here.

verses.text: has walked in my statutes, and has kept my ordinances, to deal truly; he is just, he shall surely live,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: has walked in my statutes, and has kept my ordinances, to deal truly; Arminian readers see the verdict, he shall surely live, as the LORD’s promise to one who walks in his ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase he is just, he shall surely live. They read the promise within the covenant, where life is God’s gift and obedience is its fruit and evidence.

verses.text: “If he fathers a son who is a robber who sheds blood, and who does any one of these things,
verses.arminianNotes: If he fathers a son who is a robber who sheds blood, Arminian readers see the second case: a son who rejects his father’s example and chooses violence.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that a righteous father does not guarantee a righteous son. Each generation must answer for itself, which is the point the chapter is building toward.

verses.text: or who does not do any of those things but has eaten at the mountain shrines and defiled his neighbor’s wife,
verses.arminianNotes: or who does not do any of those things but has eaten at the mountain shrines Arminian readers see the son reversing his father’s faithfulness in worship and in his treatment of his neighbor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the list mirrors the earlier one in reverse. The contrast between father and son makes the principle of individual accountability vivid.

verses.text: has wronged the poor and needy, has taken by robbery, has not restored the pledge, and has lifted up his eyes to the idols, has committed abomination,
verses.arminianNotes: has wronged the poor and needy, has taken by robbery, Arminian readers see injustice toward the vulnerable joined with idolatry, the son having committed abomination.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that oppression of the poor and idolatry appear side by side. The prophets regularly treat social injustice and false worship as twin expressions of unfaithfulness.

verses.text: has lent with interest, and has taken increase from the poor, shall he then live? He shall not live. He has done all these abominations. He shall surely die. His blood will be on him.
verses.arminianNotes: has lent with interest, and has taken increase from the poor, shall he then live? Arminian readers hear the verdict as the just outcome of a life chosen against God’s ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the solemn sentence that his blood will be on him. Responsibility rests on the violent son himself, not on his righteous father or anyone else.

verses.text: “Now, behold, if he fathers a son who sees all his father’s sins which he has done, and fears, and doesn’t do likewise,
verses.arminianNotes: who sees all his father’s sins which he has done, and fears, Arminian readers see the third case: a grandson who considers his father’s sins and chooses differently.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the word fears, suggesting reverent awareness of God. The son is not bound by his father’s path, and the text does not treat him as fated to repeat it.

verses.text: who hasn’t eaten on the mountains, hasn’t lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, hasn’t defiled his neighbor’s wife,
verses.arminianNotes: hasn’t defiled his neighbor’s wife, Arminian readers see the grandson reclaiming the faithfulness of the first generation, refusing idols and honoring marriage in his own household.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the grandson’s life repeats the pattern of the righteous man in 18:6. The list underlines that the same standard applies in every generation.

verses.text: hasn’t wronged any, hasn’t taken anything to pledge, hasn’t taken by robbery, but has given his bread to the hungry, and has covered the naked with a garment;
verses.arminianNotes: hasn’t wronged any, hasn’t taken anything to pledge, Arminian readers see justice restored in the family line through the grandson’s mercy toward the hungry and the naked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel with 18:7. Mercy toward the needy marks the grandson as one who walks in the LORD’s ways, unlike his violent father.

verses.text: who has withdrawn his hand from the poor, who hasn’t received interest or increase, has executed my ordinances, has walked in my statutes; he shall not die for the iniquity of his father. He shall surely live.
verses.arminianNotes: who has withdrawn his hand from the poor, Arminian readers see the promise that he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, but shall surely live.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the son’s life is not forfeited by his father’s sin. This is the heart of the chapter’s answer to the proverb of 18:2.

verses.text: As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, robbed his brother, and did that which is not good among his people, behold, he will die in his iniquity.
verses.arminianNotes: As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, robbed his brother, Arminian readers see justice applied to the father as well: he will die in his iniquity, not because of his son.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the verse completes the three-generation illustration. Each man stands before God on his own account, as the LORD stated in 18:4.

verses.text: “Yet you say, ‘Why doesn’t the son bear the iniquity of the father?’ When the son has done that which is lawful and right, and has kept all my statutes, and has done them, he will surely live.
verses.arminianNotes: Yet you say, ‘Why doesn’t the son bear the iniquity of the father?’ Arminian readers see the people’s objection answered by restating the principle that the righteous son will surely live.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the people seem to expect inherited guilt, perhaps to explain their own suffering. The LORD answers by affirming that obedience leads to life.

verses.text: The soul who sins, he shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be on him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be on him.
verses.arminianNotes: The soul who sins, he shall die. Arminian readers hear Deuteronomy 24:16 echoed here, Every man shall be put to death for his own sin, and see each person accountable for his own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Exodus 20:5 and Deuteronomy 5:9 speak of visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children of those who hate me. They read the texts side by side, each in its own setting.
